E052-01.notes: Object of preposition 'of' in a relative clause needs 'whom'. 'who' is the subject form; 'them' creates a comma splice (Skaters, many of them had paid... spent) since the clause becomes independent; 'whose' needs a following noun.

E052-02.notes: Original leaves 'Spending most of the 1940s on the problem.' as a fragment. B: semicolon still leaves a fragment after it. C: 'and spending' coordinates a participle with nothing parallel (no finite verb), ungrammatical. D attaches the participial phrase to the main clause correctly.

E052-03.notes: 'His first successful model' is a unique referent, so 'which he finished in 1949' is nonessential and needs a pair of commas. A has none; C and D each have only one comma, splitting subject from verb. 'which' also signals a nonrestrictive clause.

E052-04.notes: Colon after the independent clause 'combined three tasks' introduces the complete list. B: semicolon needs an independent clause after it. C: 'such as:' adds a colon after 'such as' and wrongly implies the list is partial (exactly three named). D: 'tasks that were shaving the ice' is wordy and changes meaning (tasks were actively shaving).

E052-05.notes: Only C contrasts labor and time (one driver, minutes vs. a crew, more than an hour), linking back to sentence 3. A, B, D are vague. 'In minutes' is accurate (a resurfacer takes about 10-15 minutes).

E052-06.notes: Subject is singular 'Each' (the plural 'rinks' is in the prepositional phrase), so the verb is 'was'. Past tense matches the narrative. 'have been' and 'are' are plural and also shift tense.

E052-07.notes: 'regardless of who made it' says the name is used even for machines that other makers built. A and C are unsupported. B misreads it, since the phrase says nothing about quality.

E052-08.notes: 'the figure skater Sonja Henie' uses a restrictive appositive: there are many figure skaters, so the name is essential and takes no commas. B would treat the name as nonessential, wrongly implying there is only one figure skater. C and D separate the subject from its verb with a single mark.

E052-09.notes: S9 'Within a few years' follows the 1950 Henie order. S10 'the rinks that bought a machine' depends on S9's mention of rinks placing orders. Putting S9 before S8 breaks the chronology and the move from Henie's order to broader orders. After S10 or S11 breaks the reference and the ending.
